title: Additional HTTP Status Codes

hero.subtitle: Introducing 429 Too Many Requests and other essential HTTP status codes

subtitle: Introducing 429 Too Many Requests and other essential HTTP status codes
summary: RFC 6585 adds four HTTP status codes: 428 Precondition Required, 429 Too Many Requests, 431 Request Header Fields Too Large and 511 Network Authentication Required. The best known is 429, used for rate limiting, which may carry a Retry-After header. Responses with these codes must not be stored by a cache.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6585 adds four HTTP status codes: 428 Precondition Required, 429 Too Many Requests, 431 Request Header Fields Too Large and 511 Network Authentication Required. The best known is 429, used for rate limiting, which may carry a Retry-After header. Caches must not store responses with these codes.

tldr.problem: HTTP had no standard status codes for rate limiting, required conditional requests, oversized headers or network login.
tldr.mechanism: Four new codes, 428, 429, 431 and 511, each with a defined meaning, and 429 may carry a Retry-After header.
tldr.outcome: Clients and APIs can tell these conditions apart and react correctly, especially to rate limits.

facts.label: Caching
facts.value: None of the four may be stored by a cache

today: 429 is everywhere: public APIs use it for rate limiting, and well-behaved clients back off and respect Retry-After when it is present. 431 is a common failure when cookies pile up on a domain. 428 is used by services that want to prevent lost updates with If-Match. 511 is used by some captive portals, though many portals still redirect instead. The codes are now part of the HTTP status code registry.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document specifies additional HTTP status codes for common situations that are not well served by existing codes. These codes have become essential for modern web APIs and infrastructure.

The 429 Too Many Requests status code has become one of the most important additions to HTTP, enabling standardized rate limiting across APIs worldwide. Before this RFC, APIs used various non-standard approaches to communicate rate limits.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC adds HTTP status codes for common situations that existing codes did not cover well. The most important is 429 Too Many Requests, which gives APIs a standard way to signal rate limits. Before this RFC, APIs used various non-standard approaches.

sections.title: 428 Precondition Required
sections.content:
The 428 status code indicates that the origin server requires the request to be conditional. This is used to prevent the "lost update" problem, where concurrent modifications can overwrite each other.

428 Precondition Required Example
Client request (missing If-Match):
PUT /resource HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Content-Type: application/json

{"name": "updated"}

Server response:
HTTP/1.1 428 Precondition Required
Content-Type: application/json

{"error": "If-Match header required for PUT"}

This differs from 412 Precondition Failed. A 412 means a precondition was present but evaluated to false. A 428 means a precondition was required but not present at all.
sections.plainLanguage: Status 428 means the server requires the request to be conditional, for example with an If-Match header. This prevents the lost update problem, where two clients edit the same resource and one overwrites the other. It differs from 412, which means a condition was sent but was false.

sections.title: 429 Too Many Requests
sections.content:
The 429 status code indicates that the user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time ("rate limiting"). The response representation SHOULD include details explaining the condition, and MAY include a Retry-After header indicating how long to wait.

429 Too Many Requests Example
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Content-Type: application/json
Retry-After: 60

{
  "error": "Rate limit exceeded",
  "limit": 100,
  "remaining": 0,
  "reset": 1609459200
}
Rate Limiting
APIs use 429 to enforce request quotas. Common patterns include per-second, per-minute, and per-day limits based on API key or IP address.
Retry-After
The Retry-After header tells the client when it can retry. It can specify seconds or an HTTP date.
Scope
The rate limit may apply to the user, API key, IP address, or any other classification. The response body can provide details.
sections.plainLanguage: Status 429 means the client has sent too many requests in a given time. The response should explain the limit and may include a Retry-After header saying how long to wait. APIs use it to enforce quotas per second, minute or day.

sections.title: 431 Request Header Fields Too Large
sections.content:
The 431 status code indicates that the server is unwilling to process the request because its header fields are too large. This can apply to the total size of all headers or a single header field.

Common CauseOversized cookies accumulating over time
Server LimitVaries by server and configuration
RecoveryClient should clear cookies or reduce header payload

This is a common issue with applications that set many cookies. Each request includes all matching cookies, and the cumulative size can exceed server limits. Clearing cookies for the domain typically resolves the issue.
sections.plainLanguage: Status 431 means the server refuses a request because its header fields are too large, either in total or a single field. A common cause is cookies that accumulate over time. Clearing cookies for the domain, or reducing the headers, usually fixes it.

sections.title: 511 Network Authentication Required
sections.content:
The 511 status code indicates that the client needs to authenticate to gain network access. This is used by captive portals in hotels, airports, and other public Wi-Fi networks.

511 Captive Portal Response
HTTP/1.1 511 Network Authentication Required
Content-Type: text/html

<html>
  <head><title>Network Login Required</title></head>
  <body>
    <p>You must <a href="https://login.example.net/">
    log in</a> to access the network.</p>
  </body>
</html>

The 511 status was specifically designed for captive portals, as an alternative to the common practice of using redirects or injecting content into HTTP responses, which non-browser clients cannot tell apart from a response from the real server. It helps clients distinguish between a legitimate server response and network-level authentication requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Status 511 means the client must authenticate to get network access. Captive portals in hotels, airports and other public Wi-Fi networks use it. It was designed as an alternative to redirects or injected content for sending users to a login page.
